title: Serveflow quant sensitivity and kernel arbitration lab
content:
Purpose and high-level summary:

This lab notebook captures an end-to-end serving sensitivity sweep we ran to understand how quantization format + kernel selection interact with prefix cache hit rates and request fanout in the real ServeFlow (inference pipeline) environment. The focus is not just raw token/s numbers but the combined effect on tail latency (p95/p99), user-facing QA accuracy on our internal eval set, and how a dynamic kernel arbitration policy could trade off cost vs SLA risk.

Why this is different from prior runs:
- Instead of isolated microbenching kernels, we exercised the full request path (client -> gateway routing -> cache lookup -> kernel dispatch -> KV cache behavior) using recorded production traces scaled to realistic mixes.
- Introduced a "kernel arbitration" shim that can pick kernels at request-time based on a simple SLO heuristic (latency budget, recent cache hit, and estimated token charge).
- Measured per-workload sensitivity (QA-style prompts vs long-context summarization) rather than only synthetic token streams.

Experimental setup:
- Hardware: A100-80GB and H100 nodes; tests run on a dedicated cluster matching Dedicated-2 config.
- Models: Llama-2-7B (V2), Mistral-7B-Chat (small checkpoints for latency probes).
- Quant formats: 1) INT8 via GPTQ (baseline quantized path), 2) AWQ tuned 6-bit per-channel, 3) per-layer FP8 emulation (E4M3-ish dynamic range), and 4) FP16 baseline.
- Kernels evaluated: kernlite-v1 (vector-friendly, high throughput), warp-sched (latency-optimized, less aggressive packing), vecx-prefetch (prefetch+packing tradeoffs).
- Workloads: three mixes derived from production traces: 
  - Short-chat: median tokens per request 40, high concurrency.
  - Long-summary: median tokens per request 1200, cache effectiveness low.
  - Mixed QA: median tokens 200, prefix cache hit ~60% for repeated sessions.
- Metrics captured: throughput (tokens/sec), p50/p95/p99 generation latency, QA accuracy (micro-F1 / exact-match on internal eval set), regression rate vs FP16 (delta accuracy), attachment to cost proxy (GPU seconds / 1k requests).
- Replay harness: we used replay harness RF-3212 (see linked artifacts) with jitter and realistic backpressure.

Key findings (short bullets):
- INT8 (GPTQ) delivered the highest raw throughput on kernlite-v1 (median +42% tokens/sec vs FP16) but showed the largest quality regression on long-summary prompts (-3.1% absolute QA accuracy).
- AWQ provided a middle ground: throughput +25% vs FP16 on warp-sched with quality regression ~ -0.9% on mixed QA workloads. AWQ was more stable when prefix cache hit rate increased.
- FP8 per-layer (prototype kernels) gave throughput similar to INT8 on vecx-prefetch for short-chat but had p95 latency slightly worse than INT8 due to additional normalization steps (+8ms). Quality loss was small (~ -0.6%) but more variable across prompt types.
- Kernel arbitration (simple heuristic) reduced observed QA regression for short-chat by preferentially routing low-latency-required requests to AWQ/FP8 while leaving INT8 for high-throughput background batching. This policy recovered ~0.7% QA accuracy vs blind INT8 while only costing ~6% throughput.
- Cache interplay: when prefix cache hit rate >= 60%, the effective quality delta between INT8 and AWQ shrank by ~60% (short contexts benefit more). For long-summary workloads cache hit rates are low and quantization quality dominates user-facing metrics.

Representative numbers (Llama-2-7B on A100, mixed QA workload):
- FP16 + kernlite-v1: 1,800 tokens/sec, p95 48ms, QA accuracy 83.1% (baseline).
- INT8-GPTQ + kernlite-v1: 2,560 tokens/sec, p95 68ms, QA accuracy 80.0% (-3.1% abs).
- AWQ + warp-sched: 2,250 tokens/sec, p95 62ms, QA accuracy 82.2% (-0.9% abs).
- FP8-sim + vecx-prefetch: 2,470 tokens/sec, p95 56ms, QA accuracy 82.5% (-0.6% abs).
- Kernel arbitration policy (dynamic): effective throughput 2,120 tokens/sec, p95 58ms, QA accuracy 82.8% (-0.3% abs).

Notes on variance and failure modes:
- INT8 exhibited higher sample-to-sample variance on long-tail prompts that include numeric sequences or code-like tokens; we observed hallucination spikes in 0.4% of cases.
- FP8 emulation spikes were correlated with a small set of activation patterns; these manifested as occasional token-stall microbursts leading to 1–2x p99 spikes.
- Some kernels (kernlite-v1) are aggressive on packing and can cause jitter under multiplexed workloads — we saw dispatcher queueing that amplified p99 by up to 1.8x during microbursts.

Operational implications and recommended policy draft:
- For Hosted API (PLG rapid path): default to AWQ + warp-sched for most traffic, fall back to FP16 for known high-precision evals (e.g., enterprise legal/compliance prompts). Reserve INT8 for high-throughput batch endpoints or scheduled non-critical workloads.
- For Dedicated capacity: enable dynamic kernel arbitration with a safety-first fallback to FP16/FP8 if per-request calibration fails. Use a short rolling window (30s) to detect QA drift and auto-flag a rollback.
- Routing rules: if prefix_cache_hit >= 70% and latency budget <= 80ms, prefer INT8; otherwise prefer AWQ/FP8. Expose an override knob in the route config.

Suggested additional experiments (next sprint):
- Per-layer activation clip-and-recompute: selectively dequant a few sensitivity layers (top-k layers) to see if INT8 quality gap closes without large throughput loss.
- Longer-term: incorporate a small generation-time lightweight neural filter that predicts per-request "sensitivity score" to drive kernel arbitration instead of simple heuristics.
- Kernel prewarming for FP8 paths to reduce p95 spikes observed on cold blocks.

Appendix: brief methodology notes
- All accuracy numbers measured on our internal "serveflow-eval-maingrid" dataset (2k prompts across domain mix).
- Each measurement aggregated over 5 runs of the full replay harness; we show medians above and inspect p95/p99 for tail behavior.
- Cost proxy computed as GPU-seconds per 1k requests, normalized to FP16 baseline = 1.0. INT8 cost: ~0.78, AWQ: ~0.86, FP8-sim: ~0.81.

Action items:
- (Priya) Draft route flag for AWQ default for hosted free tier by 2026-07-02.
- (Eli) Add per-layer sensitivity profiler to the replay harness (Linear RF-3344).
- (Marco) Validate FP8 kernel warmup strategy on H100 cluster and record p99 heatmaps.

Open questions / risks:
- How to surface per-request quality signals cheaply in production?
- What SLA guardrails do we require for enterprise customers who will not accept even small hallucination spikes?

Conclusion:
This batch of end-to-end experiments shows that format choice + kernel selection cannot be treated in isolation. With a modest arbitration policy and awareness of prefix cache hit rates, we can recover much of the quality lost to aggressive quantization while still realizing substantial unit-cost improvements. The next steps focus on operationalizing arbitration, per-layer exception paths, and improved FP8 kernel stability tests.
